claim: Numerous studies advocate for a rhythmic mode of perception.
source: Numerous studies advocate for a rhythmic mode of perception.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on rhythmic perception

claim: The evidence for rhythmicity in the context of hearing remains inconsistent.
source: However, the evidence in the context of hearing remains inconsistent.
evidence: Based on review of previous literature showing divergent results

claim: Divergent conclusions from previous work stem from conceptual and methodological issues.
source: We propose that the divergent conclusions drawn from previous work stem from conceptual and methodological issues.
evidence: Authors' inference based on analysis of previous literature

claim: Previous work has ambiguous assumptions regarding the origin of rhythmicity.
source: These include ambiguous assumptions regarding the origin of rhythmicity, variations in tasks and attentional demands, and differing analytical approaches for statistical testing.
evidence: Based on review of methodological approaches in previous studies

claim: The experiments involved monaural targets presented against binaural white noise backgrounds.
source: We conducted a series of experiments in which human participants performed auditory tasks involving monaural targets presented against binaural white noise backgrounds, while also recording eye movements.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design

claim: Eye movements were recorded during the experiments.
source: We conducted a series of experiments in which human participants performed auditory tasks involving monaural targets presented against binaural white noise backgrounds, while also recording eye movements.
evidence: Direct description of experimental measurements

claim: The experiments varied in whether stimuli were presented randomly or required motor initialisation.
source: These experiments varied in whether stimuli were presented randomly or required motor initialisation, the necessity of memory across trials, and the manipulation of attentional demands.
evidence: Description of experimental design variations

claim: The findings challenge the notion of universal rhythmicity in hearing.
source: Our findings challenge the notion of universal rhythmicity in hearing, but support the existence of paradigm- and ear-specific fluctuations in sensitivity and biases at multiple frequencies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Paradigm- and ear-specific fluctuations in sensitivity and biases exist at multiple frequencies.
source: Our findings challenge the notion of universal rhythmicity in hearing, but support the existence of paradigm- and ear-specific fluctuations in sensitivity and biases at multiple frequencies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: The rhythmicity for sounds in the left and right ears appears independent among participants.
source: The rhythmicity for sounds in the left and right ears appears independent among participants, and the rhythmicity in performance is possibly linked to oculomotor activity and attentional requirements.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Rhythmicity in performance is possibly linked to oculomotor activity and attentional requirements.
source: The rhythmicity for sounds in the left and right ears appears independent among participants, and the rhythmicity in performance is possibly linked to oculomotor activity and attentional requirements.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results

claim: Perception is an active process shaped by external stimuli and intrinsic states of sensory pathways.
source: Following this, perception is an active process, shaped not only by external stimuli but also by intrinsic states of the sensory pathways and their interactions with the motor system (Schroeder et al., 2008; Benedetto et al., 2020; Morillon et al., 2015; Lima et al., 2016; De Kock et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Perception is shaped by interactions between sensory pathways and the motor system.
source: Following this, perception is an active process, shaped not only by external stimuli but also by intrinsic states of the sensory pathways and their interactions with the motor system (Schroeder et al., 2008; Benedetto et al., 2020; Morillon et al., 2015; Lima et al., 2016; De Kock et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Stimuli occurring during specific moments in time are more likely to be perceived according to perceptual cycles.
source: This led to the idea of 'perceptual cycles', whereby stimuli occurring during specific moments in time are more likely to be perceived, or are perceived more accurately, compared to those during other moments (VanRullen, 2016; Latour, 1967; Pöppel, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: The rhythmic structure in neural activity along auditory pathways aligns with the multi-scale structure of vocalisations and speech.
source: In the context of hearing, this notion of a rhythmic mode of hearing is supported by the prevailing rhythmic structure in neural activity along the auditory pathways, which aligns with the typical multi-scale structure of vocalisations and speech (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Ding et al., 2016; Obleser and Kayser, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: A rhythmic mode may be the default operational mode for listening.
source: Conceptually, it has been proposed that a rhythmic mode may be the default operational mode for listening and that a continuous mode becomes engaged under conditions of prolonged vigilance or high arousal (Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Lakatos et al., 2016; Milne et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: A continuous mode becomes engaged under conditions of prolonged vigilance or high arousal.
source: Conceptually, it has been proposed that a rhythmic mode may be the default operational mode for listening and that a continuous mode becomes engaged under conditions of prolonged vigilance or high arousal (Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Lakatos et al., 2016; Milne et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Pitch judgments for tones presented on background noise vary at the scale of 6–8 Hz depending on their timing relative to the background.
source: For example, one study showed that pitch judgments for tones presented on a background noise vary at the scale of 6–8 Hz depending on their timing relative to this background (Ho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Neuroimaging studies link large-scale rhythmic activity to perceptual judgements.
source: Neuroimaging studies further support this concept by linking large-scale rhythmic activity to perceptual judgements (Ng et al., 2012; Strauß et al., 2015; Henry et al., 2016; Wöstmann et al., 2019; ten Oever and Sack, 2015; Florin et al., 2017), and in vivo recordings confirm the prominence of rhythmic changes in neural excitability and information transmission directly along the auditory pathways (Lakatos et al., 2005; Lakatos et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: In vivo recordings confirm the prominence of rhythmic changes in neural excitability along auditory pathways.
source: Neuroimaging studies further support this concept by linking large-scale rhythmic activity to perceptual judgements (Ng et al., 2012; Strauß et al., 2015; Henry et al., 2016; Wöstmann et al., 2019; ten Oever and Sack, 2015; Florin et al., 2017), and in vivo recordings confirm the prominence of rhythmic changes in neural excitability and information transmission directly along the auditory pathways (Lakatos et al., 2005; Lakatos et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: It has been difficult to obtain coherent evidence for perceptual cycles in hearing based on purely behavioural data.
source: However, it has been difficult to obtain coherent evidence for perceptual cycles in hearing based on purely behavioural data.
evidence: Based on review of previous literature

claim: Some studies reported positive results for perceptual cycles while others failed to find such or reported only weak evidence.
source: While some studies reported positive results, others failed to find such or reported only weak evidence for rhythmicity (Ho et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2017; Hickok et al., 2015; Farahbod et al., 2020; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: The reported rhythmicity varies in time scale and significance across previous listening studies.
source: Previous listening studies, for example, presented brief sounds during unstructured noise and showed that participants' judgements vary with the delay between the onset of the noise and the target. Yet, the reported rhythmicity varies in time scale and significance (Ho et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2022; Kayser, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Some studies employed binaural targets and assumed rhythmicity is present at the same frequency in monaural pathways or arises after binaural convergence.
source: Some studies employed binaural targets and hence assumed that rhythmicity is either present at the same frequency in monaural pathways or arises after binaural convergence (Hickok et al., 2015; Farahbod et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022; Kayser, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Other studies tested monaural targets and reported effects at different frequencies for each ear.
source: In contrast, other studies directly tested monaural targets and reported effects at different frequencies for each ear (Ho et al., 2019; Ho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Ear-specificity of rhythmic perceptual sampling is not unreasonable given hemisphere differences in rhythmic activity in auditory cortices.
source: Such an ear-specificity of rhythmic perceptual sampling is not unreasonable given hemisphere differences in the prominence of rhythmic activity in auditory cortices and their putative link to a functional differentiation of left and right auditory networks (Gross et al., 2013; Keitel et al., 2018; Albouy et al., 2020; Flinker et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Targets were presented monaurally and data were analysed from individual ears and when collapsing across ears.
source: In order to probe the ear-specificity of rhythmicity, we presented targets monaurally and analysed the data from individual ears, but also when collapsing across ears (Figure 2).
evidence: Description of experimental design and reference to figure

claim: Rhythmicity in behavioural data could originate from rhythmic processes in monaural auditory processes operating at different frequencies for each ear.
source: (A) Rhythmicity in behavioural data could have several origins. On the one extreme are rhythmic processes in monaural auditory processes that operate at different frequencies for sounds in each ear (left scheme).
evidence: Conceptual framework presented in Figure 1A

claim: Rhythmicity could originate from high-level processes tied to cognition that operate in the same manner on any sound.
source: On the other extreme are high-level processes possibility more tied to cognition than sensation, that operate in the same manner on any sound and which give rise to the same rhythmicity in behavioural data following monaural or binaural stimuli (right scheme).
evidence: Conceptual framework presented in Figure 1A

claim: Independent white noise was presented to each ear over a period of 1.8 s after a pseudo-random fixation period (0.3–0.5 s).
source: (B) General design of the four experiments. In each experiment, independent white noise was presented to each ear over a period of 1.8 s after a pseudo-random fixation period (0.3–0.5 s).
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Task-relevant sounds were presented monaurally at random time points between 0.3 and 1.5 s following noise onset.
source: The task-relevant sounds were presented monaurally and at random time points between 0.3 and 1.5 s following the noise onset and either comprised one (40 ms) or two (30 ms) sounds.
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Experiments 1, 2, 4 featured a tone discrimination task with a decision criterion fixed across trials.
source: Experiments 1, 2, 4 featured a tone discrimination task with a decision criterion fixed across trials (tones categorised as 'low' or 'high').
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Experiment 3 featured a within-trial discrimination of two subsequent tones.
source: Experiment 3 featured a within-trial discrimination of two subsequent tones.
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Experiments 1 and 2 differ in that sound presentation was automatically paced or required manual initialisation by the participant.
source: Experiments 1 and 2 differ in that sound presentation was automatically paced or required manual initialisation by the participant.
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Experiment 4 required participants to perform a dual task on the visual fixation dot to divert attention across sensory modalities.
source: Experiment 1 and 4 differed in that the latter also required participants to perform a dual task on in the visual fixation dot. This was intended to divert attention across sensory modalities.
evidence: Description of experimental design in Figure 1B

claim: Data with and without rhythmicity were simulated to calibrate the statistical specificity of each approach.
source: We simulated data with and without rhythmicity to calibrate the statistical specificity (false positive rate) of each approach.
evidence: Description of simulation methods in Figure 2

claim: Three approaches were tested: spectra-based, binned data analysis, and single-trial data analysis.
source: The approaches are based on the spectra derived from delay-binned data ('Spectra'), the vector strength of a rhythmic component in linear models applied to delay-binned data ('Binned') and the vector strength of a rhythmic component in linear models applied to single-trial data ('Trials').
evidence: Description of analytical approaches in Figure 2

claim: The first-level threshold was determined to result in a false-positive rate of about 0.05 when probing for rhythmicity at any frequency.
source: For each, we determined the respective first-level threshold (i.e. method-specific p-value) that results in a false-positive rate of about 0.05 when probing for rhythmicity at any frequency.
evidence: Description of statistical calibration in Figure 2

claim: Sensitivity decreases for targets presented late in the trial.
source: This illustrates temporal structure in behaviour, such as decreasing sensitivity or reaction times for targets presented late in the trial.
evidence: Observation from delay-binned data analysis

claim: Reaction times decrease for targets presented late in the trial.
source: This illustrates temporal structure in behaviour, such as decreasing sensitivity or reaction times for targets presented late in the trial.
evidence: Observation from delay-binned data analysis

claim: Temporal structure in behavioural data at multiple time scales is often observed in perceptual decision-making paradigms.
source: This is in line with previous studies reporting temporal structure in behavioural data at multiple time scales, which is often observed in perceptual decision-making paradigms and may reflect individual strategies for analysing the sensory environment, leakage in decision processes, or the urgency to respond (Kayser, 2019; Okazawa et al., 2018; Waskom et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: In experiment 1, there was a significant effect for d-prime around 2 Hz for the right ear.
source: For experiment 1, this included an effect for d-prime around 2 Hz for the right ear, for experiment 2, an effect for bias around 6.5 Hz for the left ear, and for experiment 3, an effect in d-prime around 3 Hz for the combined-ear data.
evidence: Statistical results from experiment 1

claim: In experiment 2, there was a significant effect for bias around 6.5 Hz for the left ear.
source: For experiment 1, this included an effect for d-prime around 2 Hz for the right ear, for experiment 2, an effect for bias around 6.5 Hz for the left ear, and for experiment 3, an effect in d-prime around 3 Hz for the combined-ear data.
evidence: Statistical results from experiment 2

claim: In experiment 3, there was a significant effect in d-prime around 3 Hz for the combined-ear data.
source: For experiment 1, this included an effect for d-prime around 2 Hz for the right ear, for experiment 2, an effect for bias around 6.5 Hz for the left ear, and for experiment 3, an effect in d-prime around 3 Hz for the combined-ear data.
evidence: Statistical results from experiment 3

claim: Experiments 1 and 2 differed in that trials were automatically paced (experiment 1) or self-initialised (experiment 2).
source: Remember that experiments 1 and 2 differed in that trials were automatically paced (experiment 1) or self-initialised (experiment 2), while experiments 1 and 3 differed in that the relevant stimulus information had to be compared between trials (experiment 1) or within-trials (experiment 3).
evidence: Description of experimental design differences

claim: Experiments 1 and 3 differed in that stimulus information had to be compared between trials (experiment 1) or within-trials (experiment 3).
source: Remember that experiments 1 and 2 differed in that trials were automatically paced (experiment 1) or self-initialised (experiment 2), while experiments 1 and 3 differed in that the relevant stimulus information had to be compared between trials (experiment 1) or within-trials (experiment 3).
evidence: Description of experimental design differences

claim: The effects mentioned for experiments 1-3 prevail for at least 50% of the simulated experiments.
source: This revealed that the above-mentioned effects prevail for at least 50% of the simulated experiments, corroborating their robustness within the participant sample.
evidence: Results from resampling analysis

claim: In experiment 1, sensitivity is modulated in the right ear at around 2 Hz and the left ear around 6.5 Hz with comparable prevalence.
source: For experiment 1, sensitivity is modulated in the right ear at around 2 Hz and the left ear around 6.5 Hz with comparable prevalence in multiple approaches (Spectra: 45% vs 38%; Binned: 35% vs 55%; see Figure 6).
evidence: Results from resampling analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: In experiment 1, both perceptual sensitivity and bias may be modulated in both ears at different frequencies.
source: Collectively, this suggests that, in fact both, perceptual sensitivity and bias, may be modulated and in both ears, but at different frequencies.
evidence: Inference from prevalence data analysis

claim: In experiment 2, there is considerable prevalence of an effect in sensitivity for the right ear around 2 Hz.
source: However, there is considerable prevalence of an effect in sensitivity for the right ear around 2 Hz (Spectra 38%), suggesting that also in this experiment, both ears may exhibit rhythmicity, again possibly at distinct frequencies.
evidence: Results from prevalence analysis

claim: In experiment 3, all three approaches reveal the prevalence of rhythmicity in sensitivity around 2–3 Hz for the combined-ear data.
source: For experiment 3, all three approaches reveal the prevalence of rhythmicity in sensitivity around 2–3 Hz for the combined-ear data (Spectra 44%, Binned 78%, and Trials 49%) and to a smaller degree also in the left ear (Spectra 40%, Binned 34%) without direct counterpart for the right ear at the same frequency.
evidence: Results from prevalence analysis

claim: Multiple behavioural metrics reveal a largely comparable prevalence of rhythmicity across experiments and ears.
source: Hence, based on this analysis of the data, we conclude that multiple behavioural metrics reveal a largely comparable prevalence of rhythmicity across experiments and ears, and that the precise frequencies and prevalence vary between approaches and experiments.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from prevalence analysis

claim: The precise frequencies and prevalence of rhythmicity vary between approaches and experiments.
source: Hence, based on this analysis of the data, we conclude that multiple behavioural metrics reveal a largely comparable prevalence of rhythmicity across experiments and ears, and that the precise frequencies and prevalence vary between approaches and experiments.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from prevalence analysis

claim: The two ears tend to exhibit the highest prevalence of effects at complementary frequencies.
source: This summary suggests that the two ears indeed tend to exhibit the highest prevalence of effects at complementary frequencies.
evidence: Conclusion from averaged prevalence data across experiments

claim: Peaks for sensitivity in the right ear prevail around 2 Hz and 4 Hz.
source: In particular, peaks for sensitivity in the right ear prevail around 2 Hz and 4 Hz, and for the left ear around 3 Hz and 6 Hz.
evidence: Results from averaged prevalence data

claim: Peaks for sensitivity in the left ear prevail around 3 Hz and 6 Hz.
source: In particular, peaks for sensitivity in the right ear prevail around 2 Hz and 4 Hz, and for the left ear around 3 Hz and 6 Hz.
evidence: Results from averaged prevalence data

claim: The rhythmic effects in the left and right ears may emerge in distinct groups of participants and may not be strictly linked.
source: The data also leave the possibility that the rhythmic effects in the left and right ears emerge in distinct groups of participants and may not be strictly linked.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: The correlations of co-occurrences of effects in the two ears were minimal.
source: The correlations of these co-occurrences of effects in the two ears were minimal (Spectra: r=−0.01, p=0.46, Binned: r=0.018, p=0.20, n=5000), suggesting that any rhythmicity for left and right ears may not emerge simultaneously but in part prevails in separate groups of participants.
evidence: Statistical results from correlation analysis

claim: Rhythmicity for left and right ears may not emerge simultaneously but in part prevails in separate groups of participants.
source: The correlations of these co-occurrences of effects in the two ears were minimal (Spectra: r=−0.01, p=0.46, Binned: r=0.018, p=0.20, n=5000), suggesting that any rhythmicity for left and right ears may not emerge simultaneously but in part prevails in separate groups of participants.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: Participants' sensitivity to the intensity changes of the fixation dot was high (d-prime, 3.96±0.12).
source: Their sensitivity to the intensity changes of the fixation dot was high (d-prime, 3.96±0.12, mean ± s.e.m., n=36) and they exhibited no obvious bias in that judgement (bias 0.08±0.04).
evidence: Experimental results from dual task performance

claim: Participants exhibited no obvious bias in the dual task judgement (bias 0.08±0.04).
source: Their sensitivity to the intensity changes of the fixation dot was high (d-prime, 3.96±0.12, mean ± s.e.m., n=36) and they exhibited no obvious bias in that judgement (bias 0.08±0.04).
evidence: Experimental results from dual task performance

claim: Reaction times differed significantly between blocks with and without the dual task.
source: Reaction times (with dual task 1.16+0.01 ms vs. without 1.04±0.01, t=11.3, p<10–10) and participants' bias towards one judgement differed significantly between blocks with and without the dual task (bias: 0.07±0.05 to -0.03±0.04, t=3.0, p=0.008), while sensitivity to the tone frequencies did not (d-prime: 1.52±0.06 vs 1.47±0.06, t=1.2, p=0.21).
evidence: Statistical comparison between dual task conditions

claim: Participants' bias towards one judgement differed significantly between blocks with and without the dual task.
source: Reaction times (with dual task 1.16+0.01 ms vs. without 1.04±0.01, t=11.3, p<10–10) and participants' bias towards one judgement differed significantly between blocks with and without the dual task (bias: 0.07±0.05 to -0.03±0.04, t=3.0, p=0.008), while sensitivity to the tone frequencies did not (d-prime: 1.52±0.06 vs 1.47±0.06, t=1.2, p=0.21).
evidence: Statistical comparison between dual task conditions

claim: Sensitivity to the tone frequencies did not differ significantly between blocks with and without the dual task.
source: Reaction times (with dual task 1.16+0.01 ms vs. without 1.04±0.01, t=11.3, p<10–10) and participants' bias towards one judgement differed significantly between blocks with and without the dual task (bias: 0.07±0.05 to -0.03±0.04, t=3.0, p=0.008), while sensitivity to the tone frequencies did not (d-prime: 1.52±0.06 vs 1.47±0.06, t=1.2, p=0.21).
evidence: Statistical comparison between dual task conditions

claim: The direct statistical comparison between dual task conditions revealed no significant difference for the combined-ear data.
source: The direct statistical comparison between conditions revealed no significant difference (at p<0.05 for the combined-ear data; paired t-tests, corrected for multiple tests across frequencies), and the prevalence of significant effects in variations of the participant sample was low for the unilateral data.
evidence: Statistical results from dual task comparison

claim: For sensitivity in the combined ear data, the prevalence of significant effects was nearly 40% around 4 Hz and 8 Hz.
source: However, for the sensitivity in the combined ear data the prevalence of significant effects was nearly 40% around 4 Hz and 8 Hz, suggesting that at these frequencies a subgroup of participants tends to exhibit more rhythmicity when performing the dual task.
evidence: Results from prevalence analysis of dual task effects

claim: A subgroup of participants tends to exhibit more rhythmicity when performing the dual task at 4 Hz and 8 Hz.
source: However, for the sensitivity in the combined ear data the prevalence of significant effects was nearly 40% around 4 Hz and 8 Hz, suggesting that at these frequencies a subgroup of participants tends to exhibit more rhythmicity when performing the dual task.
evidence: Inference from prevalence analysis

claim: No significant difference was found between trials with larger or smaller pupil size prior to the target.
source: When splitting trials by trial-wise pupil dilation, we found no significant difference between trials with larger or smaller pupil size prior to the target in the specific participant sample (Figure 8B; left panels).
evidence: Statistical results from pupil size analysis

claim: The prevalence of significant effects related to pupil dilation was very low.
source: In support of no relation between pupil dilation and rhythmicity, we also found that the prevalence of significant effects was very low (right panels).
evidence: Results from prevalence analysis of pupil effects

claim: Trials with less fixation stability had significantly stronger rhythmic effect sizes for sensitivity around 3.5 Hz than trials with more fixation stability.
source: However, when splitting the data by the trial-wise fixation stability, we found that trials with less fixation stability had significantly stronger rhythmic effect sizes for sensitivity around 3.5 Hz than trials with more fixation stability (at p<0.05; Figure 8C).
evidence: Statistical results from fixation stability analysis

claim: The prevalence of significant effects in the combined-ear data among participant samples was 64% at 3.5 Hz for fixation stability effects.
source: Furthermore, the prevalence of significant effects in the combined-ear data among participant samples was higher (64% at 3.5 Hz).
evidence: Results from prevalence analysis of fixation stability effects

claim: Rhythmicity in behaviour seems to be more expressed when overall eye mobility is larger.
source: This suggests that rhythmicity in behaviour seems to be more expressed when overall eye mobility is larger and underscores an influence of (oculo-)motor behaviour.
evidence: Inference from fixation stability analysis

claim: The number of actual saccadic eye movements was low and amounted to an average of 0.79±0.1 per trial.
source: The number of actual saccadic eye movements was low and amounted to an average of 0.79±0.1 (mean ± s.e.m) per trial.
evidence: Measurement from eye tracking data

claim: Any influence of eye mobility is likely linked to microsaccadic behaviour or drifts and not overt large saccades.
source: Hence, any influence of eye mobility is likely linked to microsaccadic behaviour or drifts and not overt large saccades.
evidence: Inference from eye movement data

claim: Task difficulty was maintained around a similar level throughout the experiment by adjusting stimulus parameters.
source: The experiments relied on a design in which the task difficulty was maintained around a similar level throughout the experiment. This was implemented by adjusting, where necessary, the stimulus parameters to maintain a comparable level of correct responses (between 69 and 80% on average over 30 trials).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: At the group-level, stimulus parameters did not differ systematically between the start and end of experiments 1, 2, and 4.
source: While the individual participant and ear-specific time courses of stimulus parameters exhibited some fluctuations and sometimes trends reflecting learning, at the group-level these did not differ systematically between the start and end of each experiment for experiment 1 (mean ± s.e.m. change in parameters –1.13±1.46 dB, t=−0.77, p=0.45), experiment 2 (-0.88±2.17 dB, t=−0.40, p=0.68) and experiment 4 (0.08±0.04, t=1.90, p=0.56), while the stimulus intensity was significantly reduced.
evidence: Statistical analysis of stimulus parameter changes

claim: The present data speak against the presence of a mechanism that results in mandatory rhythmicity that governs auditory perception per se.
source: In our view, the present data speak against the presence of a mechanism that results in mandatory rhythmicity that governs auditory perception per se.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of overall results

claim: The present data support the existence of paradigm-specific effects that pertain to sensitivity or response biases independently.
source: Rather, the present data support the existence of paradigm-specific effects that pertain to sensitivity or response biases independently and which may emerge at different frequencies for each ear.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of overall results

claim: Paradigm-specific effects may emerge at different frequencies for each ear.
source: Rather, the present data support the existence of paradigm-specific effects that pertain to sensitivity or response biases independently and which may emerge at different frequencies for each ear.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of overall results

claim: Multiple processes including temporal entrainment, neural adaptation, temporally predictive processes, and motor-related processes interact to shape auditory perception.
source: In line with other recent work, we speculate that multiple processes, including temporal entrainment, neural adaptation, temporally predictive processes, and motor-related processes interact to shape auditory perception (L'Hermite and Zoefel, 2023).
evidence: Speculation based on current results and previous literature

claim: Specific paradigms tap into a unique combination of perceptual and motor requirements, which may explain the diversity of previous results on the rhythmicity of hearing.
source: Given that specific paradigms tap into a unique combination of perceptual and motor requirements, this may explain the diversity of previous results on the rhythmicity of hearing.
evidence: Authors' interpretation to explain divergent literature

claim: Data were collected from four experiments in which adult volunteers participated after providing informed consent.
source: We collected data from four experiments in which adult volunteers participated after providing informed consent.
evidence: Description of participant recruitment

claim: All participants had self-reported normal vision and hearing.
source: All participants had self-reported normal vision and hearing and none indicated a history of neurological disorders.
evidence: Description of participant inclusion criteria

claim: None of the participants indicated a history of neurological disorders.
source: All participants had self-reported normal vision and hearing and none indicated a history of neurological disorders.
evidence: Description of participant inclusion criteria

claim: The procedures were approved by the ethics committee of Bielefeld University (Nr. 2024–037).
source: Participants were compensated for their time and the procedures were approved by the ethics committee of Bielefeld University (Nr. 2024–037).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: The a priori sample size for each experiment was set to n=25.
source: We set the a priori sample size for each experiment to n=25.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: The actual sample sizes for experiments 1–3 were slightly higher than 25 due to parallel data collection.
source: Due to parallel data collection, the actual sample sizes for experiments 1–3 were slightly higher.
evidence: Description of actual sample sizes

claim: For experiment 4, more data were collected due to technical problems with eye tracking.
source: For experiment 4, we collected more data, in part due to technical problems with also collecting eye tracking data (see below).
evidence: Explanation of sample size for experiment 4

claim: The experiments were performed in a darkened and soundproof booth.
source: The experiments were performed in a darkened and soundproof booth (E: Box; Desone, Germany).
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: Acoustic stimuli were presented over Sennheiser DH200Pro headphones.
source: Acoustic stimuli were presented over headphones (Sennheiser DH200Pro).
evidence: Description of experimental equipment

claim: Stimulus presentation was controlled using the Psychophysics Toolbox (Version 3.0.14) using MATLAB (Version R2017a).
source: Stimulus presentation was controlled using the Psychophysics Toolbox (Version 3.0.14) using MATLAB (Version R2017a; The MathWorks, Inc, Natick, MA).
evidence: Description of experimental software

claim: In experiment 1, target tones lasted 40 ms with 5 ms cosine ramps and had frequencies of 2048 Hz and 1024 Hz.
source: Target tones lasted 40 ms (with 5 ms cosine ramps) and had frequencies of 2048 Hz and 1024 Hz.
evidence: Description of stimulus parameters for experiment 1

claim: Target tones were presented at random delays between 300 ms and 1500 ms from the onset of the background noise.
source: Target tones were presented at random delays between 300 ms and 1500 ms from the onset of the background noise (sampled uniformly).
evidence: Description of experimental timing

claim: Background noises had an r.m.s level of 65 dB SPL.
source: Background noises were generated on each trial independently for each ear and had an r.m.s level of 65 dB SPL.
evidence: Description of stimulus parameters

claim: Each participant in experiment 1 performed 8 blocks of 190 trials in one session, resulting in 380 trials per frequency and ear.
source: Each participant performed 8 blocks of 190 trials in one session, resulting in 380 trials per frequency and ear.
evidence: Description of experimental design for experiment 1

claim: Data were collected from 27 participants in experiment 1.
source: For this experiment, we collected data from 27 participants.
evidence: Statement of sample size for experiment 1

claim: Data were collected from 26 participants in experiment 2.
source: For this experiment, we collected data from 26 participants.
evidence: Statement of sample size for experiment 2

claim: In experiment 3, target stimuli consisted of two 30 ms tones separated by 40 ms and presented at 60 dB SPL.
source: Background noises were as in experiment 1 but target stimuli consisted of two 30 ms tones separated by 40 ms and presented at 60 dB SPL.
evidence: Description of stimulus parameters for experiment 3

claim: Participants in experiment 3 performed eight blocks of 190 trials.
source: Participants performed eight blocks of 190 trials and we collected data from 26 participants.
evidence: Description of experimental design for experiment 3

claim: Data were collected from 26 participants in experiment 3.
source: Participants performed eight blocks of 190 trials and we collected data from 26 participants.
evidence: Statement of sample size for experiment 3

claim: Each participant in experiment 4 performed 16 blocks comprising 130 trials, split over two sessions taking place on different days.
source: Each participant performed 16 blocks comprising 130 trials, split over two sessions taking place on different days.
evidence: Description of experimental design for experiment 4

claim: Data were collected from a total of 36 participants in experiment 4.
source: Because of technical difficulties in obtaining stable eye movement recordings in some participants and sessions (e.g. resulting from reflections on lenses, etc.), we collected data from a total of 36 participants.
evidence: Statement of sample size for experiment 4

claim: Eye tracking data were recorded from the left eye using an EyeLink 1000 plus eye-tracking system.
source: Eye tracking data were recorded from the left eye using an EyeLink 1000 plus eye-tracking system (SR Research) with sampling rate of 500 Hz (for 18 participants) or 2000 Hz (17 participants).
evidence: Description of eye tracking equipment and parameters

claim: Outliers in the behavioural data were determined as trials with very short (<150 ms) or long reaction times (>2.5 s).
source: Outliers in the behavioural data were determined as trials with very short (<150 ms) or long reaction times (>2.5 s).
evidence: Description of data preprocessing criteria

claim: 1424±17 trials were retained for experiment 1 after removing outliers.
source: Effectively, we retained 1424±17 (mean ± s.e.m.) for experiment 1, 1435±11 for experiment 2, 1490±8 for experiment 3, and 1865±23 for experiment 4.
evidence: Statement of retained trial counts after preprocessing

claim: Only participants with at least 600 trials with good behavioural and eye-tracking data were retained for eye tracking analysis.
source: We then retained only those participants with at least 600 trials with good behavioural and eye-tracking data. This was the case for 30 participants (with 1216±67 trials on average).
evidence: Description of data inclusion criteria for eye tracking analysis

claim: 30 participants were retained for eye tracking analysis with 1216±67 trials on average.
source: We then retained only those participants with at least 600 trials with good behavioural and eye-tracking data. This was the case for 30 participants (with 1216±67 trials on average).
evidence: Statement of sample size and trial counts for eye tracking analysis

claim: The data were binned by the effective delay between background onset and target using equally spaced bins of 60 ms duration.
source: As a first step, we binned the data by the effective delay between background onset and target. We relied on equally spaced bins of 60 ms duration, resulting in 20 bins covering delays from 0 to 1200 ms.
evidence: Description of data analysis method

claim: 20 bins covering delays from 0 to 1200 ms were used in the binned analysis.
source: We relied on equally spaced bins of 60 ms duration, resulting in 20 bins covering delays from 0 to 1200 ms.
evidence: Description of data analysis parameters

claim: Frequency spectra were computed at effective frequencies between 1.05 Hz and 8.1 Hz at steps of about 0.2 Hz.
source: Based on these parameters, frequency spectra were computed at effective frequencies between 1.05 Hz and 8.1 Hz at steps of about 0.2 Hz (resulting in similar frequencies as used for the other approaches below).
evidence: Description of spectral analysis parameters

claim: Surrogate spectra were obtained for each participant by generating a distribution of 10,000 spectra based on auto-regressive processes of order 1.
source: These were obtained for each participant and metric by generating a distribution of 10,000 spectra based on auto-regressive processes of order 1.
evidence: Description of surrogate data generation method

claim: Linear models comprised an offset, a linear influence of delay, a u/v shaped influence, and a rhythmic predictor consisting of sine and cosine components.
source: Effectively, we described the data using the following terms in a linear model assuming normally distributed data and an identical link function: an offset, a linear influence of delay, a u/v shaped influence reflecting changes in behavioural data tied to the duration of the overall period of target uncertainty (here using a frequency of 0.5 Hz), and a rhythmic predictor consisting of the sine and cosine component at a specific frequency.
evidence: Description of linear model structure

claim: Vector strength was defined as the arithmetic mean of the squared betas for the sine and cosine components.
source: For each participant, we then derived the vector strength of the rhythmic predictor, defined as the arithmetic mean of the squared betas for the sine and cosine components.
evidence: Definition of vector strength metric

claim: For single-trial data, frequencies between 1.2 Hz and 12 Hz were tested.
source: As the single trial data effectively allow a higher temporal resolution compared to the binned data, we here tested frequencies between 1.2 Hz and 12 Hz (with steps of 0.8 Hz between 8 and 12 Hz).
evidence: Description of frequency range for single-trial analysis

claim: Data for a sample of 25 participants with 700 trials each were simulated to calibrate analysis approaches.
source: Practically, we simulated data for a sample of 25 participants, with 700 trials each. This corresponds to a sample size and trial count similar to the actual data, matching the analysis of individual ears.
evidence: Description of simulation parameters

claim: 1000 samples of participants (virtual experiments) were simulated for each parameter setting.
source: For each parameter setting (see below), we simulated 1000 samples of participants (i.e. virtual experiments).
evidence: Description of simulation procedure

claim: Bootstrapping was used to repeatedly draw participant samples from the entire sample to determine the percentage of simulations that yield a significant effect at each frequency.
source: We used bootstrapping to repeatedly draw participant samples from the entire sample (e.g. for experiment 1, we sampled 26 participants at random with replacement from the pool of 26 participants collected). We then determined the percentage of simulations that yield a significant effect at each frequency.
evidence: Description of bootstrapping procedure

claim: The bootstrapping approach provides an estimate of the reproducibility of effects across random variations in the participant sample.
source: These estimates of effect prevalence are shown in Figure 6 and provide an estimate of the reproducibility of effects across random variations in the participant sample.
evidence: Explanation of bootstrapping purpose

claim: The bootstrapping approach avoids potentially biased conclusions drawn from one single sample of participants.
source: This approach to investigating the prevalence of a specific (significant) effect in the participant sample has the advantage that it avoids potentially biased conclusions drawn from one single sample of participants and provides a quantification of how consistent an effect is within a population of participants.
evidence: Explanation of bootstrapping advantages
